evidenceLayer.description: Names what may count as a trace of practice (forms), who is competent to record it and what their record warrants (observer types), and the rules that govern when a form satisfies a descriptor (admissibility). Every component node names its admissible forms and competent observers inline.

forms.name: Learner-authored trace
forms.definition: A record the learner produced during the work — writing, sketch, annotation, message, saved revision, spoken note — attributable to the learner and existing independently of any later retelling.

forms.name: Artifact state
forms.definition: The artifact itself, or a preserved earlier state of it. Nobody authored it as evidence; it is the work. A kept draft, a prior version, a photograph of a build mid-assembly.

forms.name: System record
forms.definition: A timestamp, version history, submission event, access change, or other trace produced automatically by the environment the work happened in, without the learner or an observer choosing to create it.

forms.name: Observation record
forms.definition: A contemporaneous account by someone present while the practice occurred — a teacher's note, a peer's log, a caption written by an adult who watched. Its warrant is presence, not judgment.

forms.name: Audience response
forms.definition: A record of what a real audience or user did or said on encountering the work. Distinct from the learner's account of how the audience reacted.

forms.name: Learner retrospective account
forms.definition: The learner's after-the-fact explanation — a reflection, an oral defense, an interview answer. Admissible, and often the richest form, but the weakest standing alone because nothing independent constrains it.

observers.name: Self
observers.definition: The learner is the observer of their own practice.
warrants: what the learner did, as the learner represents it
the learner's reasons for a choice
doesNotWarrant: that the descriptor is satisfied at the named band

observers.name: Recipient
observers.definition: An adult who received the finished artifact without having been present while the work happened, and records what they received and when. A parent handed a completed drawing; a coach sent a photo of a build they did not watch.
warrants: that the artifact exists and was received at a stated time
the learner's authorship as reported to the recipient, not as observed
doesNotWarrant: that the descriptor is satisfied at the named band
how the work was made, or by what process
mustRecord: the recipient's relationship to the learner
that authorship is reported rather than observed

observers.name: Witness
observers.definition: An adult or peer who was present while the work happened and records what they saw. A parent, a family member, a classmate, a teacher acting in a presence role rather than an assessment role.
warrants: who did the work (authorship and presence)
doesNotWarrant: that the descriptor is satisfied at the named band
the quality or level of the practice
mustRecord: the witness's relationship to the learner

observers.name: Attester
observers.definition: An observer with assessment standing in the context — teacher, coach, assessor, reviewer — who judges that a descriptor is satisfied and is accountable for that judgment.
warrants: that the descriptor is satisfied at the named band
doesNotWarrant: practices outside the attester's own observation or the retained record
mustRecord: the evidence the judgment rests on

observers.name: Automated derivation
observers.definition: A rule or model that infers a tag from retained records with no human observer in the loop.
warrants: only what its inputs warrant, never more
doesNotWarrant: that the descriptor is satisfied at the named band
anything its inputs do not contain
mustRecord: the deriving system's identifier and version
a confidence value where the derivation is not deterministic

admissibility.name: Disclosure
admissibility.rule: Every claim that a code was demonstrated records at least one evidence form and exactly one observer type. A tag missing either is not OMBS-conformant and must not be reported as OMBS evidence.

admissibility.name: Sequence
admissibility.rule: A descriptor making a temporal claim — before, revises, predicts before test, later — requires at least one evidence form that existed during the work (OMBS.EF.LA, OMBS.EF.AR, OMBS.EF.SR, OMBS.EF.OB). A learner retrospective account alone (OMBS.EF.LR) does not establish sequence.

admissibility.name: Response
admissibility.rule: A descriptor claiming something about what an audience or user did requires OMBS.EF.AC. The learner's report of an audience reaction is a retrospective account and does not satisfy it alone.

admissibility.name: No inflation
admissibility.rule: A claim is reported at the weakest warrant in its chain. Witness records and automated derivations may support an attested claim but cannot produce one; only OMBS.OB.AT yields an attested claim. Reports must name which warrant a claim carries.

admissibility.name: Conservative derivation
admissibility.rule: An automated derivation (OMBS.OB.AD) emits no tag when its inputs are ambiguous, records the deriving system's identifier and version, and is reproducible from the retained record. A missed tag is a tolerable error; an unearned tag is not.

admissibility.name: Standing
admissibility.rule: An attested claim MUST record the assessment role under which it was made and the basis the judgment rests on. Assessment standing is conferred by that role in the context; it is never conferred by presence, by household relationship, or by having done the work. A learner judging their own practice (OMBS.OB.SF) and a parent or guardian judging their own child's (OMBS.OB.WT) MUST NOT be recorded as OMBS.OB.AT whatever role a system assigns them: their records may support an attested claim but MUST NOT be reported as one. An adult who was not present while the work happened is a recipient (OMBS.OB.RC), never a witness: presence is part of what a witness warrants and cannot be supplied after the fact.

conformance.description: What it means for an implementation to be OMBS-conformant. Two levels; Extended is a wider scope, not a better grade. Self-declared, never certified. See STANDARD.md §1.7.
conformance.migrationNote: The Core spine went from five Shared Practices to seven in 0.4.0 with the addition of OMBS.S.DG and OMBS.S.RV. The spine is broken once, in one version, rather than in two consecutive minors. No code is renamed or retired and no v0.3.0 tag becomes wrong; what changes is what a Core declaration asserts. An implementation that keeps declaring "OMBS v0.3.0, Core" stays accurate and needs no work. Migrating means adding both codes to the emitted set; where a practice was not observed it is reported as no evidence yet, never as a deficit. OMBS.S.RV will read as no-evidence-yet for any programme whose projects all begin and end inside one unit, which describes the programme rather than the learners. An adopter who cannot emit them and will not stay on 0.3.0 declares "Core (partial)" and names the missing dimensions. See STANDARD.md §1.7.

domains.name: Shared Practices
domains.description: Practices common to both making and building. Every project worth assessing exercises at least three.

dimensions.name: Define
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner identifies what they intend to make or build, for whom, and against what success criteria, before significant work begins. They revise the definition as understanding deepens.

components.descriptor: With prompting, the learner states what they will make or build and names at least one person who will see or use it.
The learner records, before substantial work begins, a written or spoken statement naming (a) the artifact, (b) the intended audience or user, and (c) at least one criterion for success.
The learner produces a written intent statement with two or more success criteria, and revises that statement at least once during the project, with the revision dated or otherwise traceable.

The learner frames the intent in tension with stated constraints (time, budget, materials, audience access) and defends scope choices in writing or in conversation against at least one feasible alternative scope considered and rejected.

dimensions.name: Draft
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner produces preliminary, low-stakes versions of the artifact — sketches, prototypes, outlines, mock-ups — that make assumptions visible before commitment to final form.

components.descriptor: The learner produces a sketch, model, or rough version before producing the final artifact, when prompted.
The learner produces at least two distinct drafts and can point to specific differences between them.
The learner produces drafts at multiple grain sizes (e.g., outline before paragraph, rough cardboard before final material) and annotates points where decisions were made.

The learner produces drafts that include explicit alternatives carried forward into testing, not only the path eventually chosen, and documents which alternatives were eliminated and on what evidence.

dimensions.name: Test
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner exposes the work to evidence — feedback from a real audience, performance against criteria, behavior under intended use — and treats the result as information, not judgment.

components.descriptor: The learner shows the work to at least one person other than the teacher and reports what that person did or said.
The learner tests the artifact against the success criterion stated in S.DF and records what happened in writing, sketch, or recording.

The learner designs tests that exercise at least two of the success criteria, conducts them with a real audience or in a realistic use scenario, and distinguishes findings driven by the test from confounds.

The learner designs at least one test capable of falsifying a key assumption of the work, conducts it, and reports negative results faithfully — including when the result reflects unfavorably on the learner's prior choices.
With prompting, the learner names the part they are least sure will work and tries that part first, before making the rest.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. The cited work is engineering literature and is not evidence about children; no source is claimed for the band placements, which are proposed observables. See STANDARD.md epistemic-status note.

components.descriptor: The learner names one thing the work depends on being true, tests that thing before building the parts that depend on it, and records what happened.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. The cited work is engineering literature and is not evidence about children; no source is claimed for the band placements, which are proposed observables. See STANDARD.md epistemic-status note.

components.descriptor: The learner lists at least two assumptions the work rests on, ranks them by what it would cost to find out late that one was wrong, records the ranking before testing, and tests the highest-cost assumption first.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. The cited work is engineering literature and is not evidence about children; no source is claimed for the band placements, which are proposed observables. See STANDARD.md epistemic-status note.

components.descriptor: Before substantial building begins, the learner records which assumption would waste the most effort if it failed late and why, tests that assumption first, and reports what the result changed about the plan — including the case where the assumption held and the ordering cost nothing.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. The cited work is engineering literature and is not evidence about children; no source is claimed for the band placements, which are proposed observables. See STANDARD.md epistemic-status note.

dimensions.name: Diagnose
dimensions.anchorStatement: Before changing the work, the learner locates what is causing the problem — reproducing it in the smallest setting that still shows it, and changing one thing at a time so the result can be attributed to the change.
dimensions.epistemicStatus: Proposed observable, not validated. The constructs have empirical support — Chen & Klahr (1999) for control-of-variables acquisition and transfer in 7- to 10-year-olds, Klahr & Carver (1988) for transfer from explicit debugging objectives, Zimmerman (2007) for the developmental picture — but none of those studies measures these observables, none was conducted on making and building work across mediums, and no study validates the band placements. Treat evidence tagged to OMBS.S.DG as exploratory; the band boundaries are the part most likely to move. See STANDARD.md §4.4.

components.descriptor: When something does not work, the learner tries it again after changing one thing and keeping the rest the same, and says with prompting whether that change made a difference.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice and, for Chen & Klahr, the plausibility of the K-2/3-5 placement. No cited study measures these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.4.

components.descriptor: The learner narrows the problem to a smaller part of the work that still shows it — one paragraph, one section, one component, one step — tests that part on its own, and records which part the problem is in.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice and, for Chen & Klahr, the plausibility of the K-2/3-5 placement. No cited study measures these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.4.

components.descriptor: Before making a change, the learner states what they think is causing the problem; then changes one thing at a time while leaving the rest as it was, recording for each try what was changed and what happened, so the result can be attributed to that change rather than to several at once.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice and, for Chen & Klahr, the plausibility of the K-2/3-5 placement. No cited study measures these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.4.

components.descriptor: The learner keeps an unchanged copy of the work that still shows the problem, compares it against the changed copy to confirm that the change is what fixed it, and reports at least one cause they suspected first and ruled out, naming the evidence that ruled it out.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice and, for Chen & Klahr, the plausibility of the K-2/3-5 placement. No cited study measures these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.4.

dimensions.name: Revisit
dimensions.anchorStatement: After a piece of work has stopped — set aside, declared finished, or abandoned — the learner chooses to return to it, does further work on it, and can say what made them stop and what brought them back.
dimensions.epistemicStatus: Proposed observable, not validated. Azevedo (2011) grounds the claim that stopping and resuming is the normal shape of sustained practice rather than a deficit; Barron (2006) grounds self-initiation across settings and does not address return. Neither measures these observables, neither studied a K-12 cohort across bands, and no study validates the band placements. The K-2 band is the placement most in need of comment. See STANDARD.md §4.5.

components.descriptor: Given a free choice of what to work on, the learner picks a piece of their own work that they had stopped and not worked on for at least a week, does more on it, and says with prompting one reason they picked that piece rather than starting something new.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. Azevedo (2011) supports recurrence and the birth/death of engagement; Barron (2006) supports self-initiated sustained projects and does not address returning to abandoned work. Neither is a K-12 study across bands and neither validates these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.5.
components.citationsTodo: Developmental claim only: no source places revisiting at a grade band, and none validates these descriptors. The K-2 band is the least supported — the gap a five-year-old can hold in mind is unknown. See STANDARD.md §4.5.

components.descriptor: The learner returns by their own choice to a piece of their own work that had been set aside, does further work on it, and names both what had stopped them and what brought them back.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. Azevedo (2011) supports recurrence and the birth/death of engagement; Barron (2006) supports self-initiated sustained projects and does not address returning to abandoned work. components.descriptor: Returning to a project they had abandoned, the learner names what stopped it, what has changed since that makes returning worth doing, and what they will do differently this time; if they work on it and then set it aside again, naming why satisfies this descriptor as fully as continuing does.

Neither is a K-12 study across bands and neither validates these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.5.

components.descriptor: The learner chooses one abandoned project from among two or more candidates, states the grounds for choosing it over the others, does further work on it, and names at least one thing they can do now that they could not do when the work stopped.
components.citationScope: Grounds the practice only. Azevedo (2011) supports recurrence and the birth/death of engagement; Barron (2006) supports self-initiated sustained projects and does not address returning to abandoned work. Neither is a K-12 study across bands and neither validates these descriptors. See STANDARD.md §4.5.

dimensions.name: Iterate
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner uses test results to revise, defending which feedback is acted on and which is set aside, with reasons.

components.descriptor: After receiving feedback, the learner tries the work again with at least one observable change.
The learner names one change made between drafts and the feedback or test result that drove it.
The learner explains, in writing or conversation, which feedback was acted on, which was set aside, and the reason for each decision.
The learner iterates across structurally distinct alternatives (not only polish or refinement of one direction) and documents abandoned directions with the evidence that led to abandonment.

dimensions.name: Share
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner makes the artifact and the process behind it accessible to an audience beyond the assessor, in a form appropriate to that audience.

components.descriptor: The learner presents the artifact to an audience beyond the teacher (classmates, family, school community), with adult support as needed.
The learner adapts the artifact or its presentation for an audience beyond the teacher and explains one adaptation made.
The learner reaches an audience they identified in S.DF and documents the audience's response in a form appropriate to the audience.

The learner publishes the artifact to a sustained public or community audience with attention to access (who can find it, who can use it), rights (attribution, licensing), and provision for follow-on use or remixing.

dimensions.name: AI-Independence
dimensions.anchorStatement: Where AI tools were used in producing the artifact, the learner can show what they kept, what they changed, and what they rejected, with reasons. Intention, voice, and the judgment behind tradeoffs remain the learner's.
dimensions.appliesWhen: AI tools were used in any substantive way (drafting, ideation, rendering, code generation, translation, summarization). Reported as not applicable when no AI tools were used.

components.descriptor: The learner points to at least one part of the work they decided themselves and at least one part the tool produced, with adult support as needed for the disclosure.
The learner discloses where AI tools were used, names at least one output they kept and at least one they changed or rejected, and gives a reason for each in their own words.

The learner maintains a record across the project that, for each substantive AI use, includes the prompt or request made, the output received, and what was kept, changed, or rejected — each kept or changed item paired with a reason in the learner's own words.

The learner can defend, in writing or conversation, that the artifact's intention, voice, and key tradeoffs would still stand if the AI-generated portions were removed; or, where they would not, names specifically what would be lost and why the loss is acceptable for the stated audience and purpose.

dimensions.componentRole: One-directional. Evidence gathered for a sub-dimension MAY be reported at this level where it satisfies the parent descriptor; satisfying every sub-dimension at a band does NOT by itself satisfy the parent component (at 9-12 it demonstrably does not — OMBS.S.AI.912.1 requires a counterfactual defense none of the four 9-12 sub-descriptors produces). Retained unchanged from v0.2.0 so existing tags stay valid.

subDimensions.name: Direction
subDimensions.anchorStatement: The learner, not the tool, decides what is to be made and what is asked of the tool. Requests made to an AI trace back to the learner's own stated intent.

components.descriptor: Before the tool is asked for anything, the learner says what they want to make, and an adult records the learner's request in the learner's own words.
The request the learner made to the tool is retained, and the learner points to the part of their own intent statement (S.DF) that the request was meant to serve.

For at least two substantive AI uses, the retained record shows the learner narrowing or redirecting the request after seeing an output, and the learner names what about their own goal drove the change — not that the output was bad.
The learner names at least one part of the work they deliberately did not ask the tool to do, and defends that choice by reference to what they intended to own or learn in the work.

subDimensions.name: Appraisal
subDimensions.anchorStatement: The learner judges each substantive AI output against criteria they can state, and the decision to keep, change, or reject it is recorded with its reason.

components.descriptor: Shown an output from the tool, the learner says whether it is what they wanted and gives one reason ("too long," "that isn't my dog"), and an adult records the exchange. Using the output without saying anything about it does not satisfy this descriptor.

For at least one AI output the learner records a decision — kept, changed, or rejected — with a reason that refers to their audience, purpose, or success criterion rather than to whether the output was good. A keep recorded without a reason — a silent keep — does not satisfy this descriptor; a reasoned keep does.

Every substantive AI output in the retained record carries a kept, changed, or rejected decision with a reason in the learner's own words, and at least one reason cites evidence from testing (S.TS) rather than preference alone. An output kept silently counts as carrying no decision.

The learner identifies at least one AI output they first accepted and later revised or rejected, names the evidence that changed their judgment, and states the criterion the output had failed. Where the earlier acceptance was a silent keep, the learner says so and names what they had not checked at the time.

subDimensions.name: Attribution
subDimensions.anchorStatement: The record maps parts of the artifact to where they came from — learner-authored, AI-generated, AI-assisted then revised, or sourced elsewhere — at a granularity a reader can check against the artifact.

components.descriptor: The learner points at the artifact and shows one part they made and one part the tool made, and an adult records which is which.
The learner discloses, in a form attached to the artifact, that AI was used and names at least one specific part of the artifact it produced or helped produce.

The artifact carries an origin note covering each substantive part — learner-authored, AI-generated, AI-assisted then revised, or sourced elsewhere — and a reader can match each claim to the part of the artifact it describes.

The learner's disclosure states the level of AI involvement for the work as a whole and for each major component, uses a stated disclosure scheme (a local policy, a publisher requirement, or a published scale), and is accurate against the retained working record.

subDimensions.name: Trajectory
subDimensions.anchorStatement: Across the work, what the learner delegates to the tool changes, and the learner can say what they took over and why.

components.descriptor: The learner names one thing they asked the tool to do earlier and did themselves later, or the reverse, and an adult confirms it against the earlier record.
Across at least two points in the project the retained record shows a part the learner first delegated to the tool and later did themselves, and the learner says what changed.

The learner compares AI use at two points in the project, or across two projects, names what they have taken over and what they still delegate, and gives a reason for each that refers to what they can now do unaided.

The learner identifies a capability they built by deliberately withdrawing AI support from part of the work, names how they would know the capability transferred to a new task, and reports what happened when they tried.

subDimensions.appliesWhen: The work contains at least two substantive AI uses. Reported as not applicable where it contains only one, since trajectory needs two observation points to be observable.

domains.name: Making
domains.description: Practice of bringing into existence an artifact intended for an audience and shaped by a purpose.

dimensions.name: Audience awareness
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner identifies a specific audience for the artifact, characterizes that audience by relevant traits (age, prior knowledge, context of encounter), and adapts the work to fit.

components.descriptor: The learner names a specific person, group, or class as the intended audience for the artifact.
The learner names at least one audience trait (age, prior knowledge, interest) and points to a choice in the artifact shaped by that trait.
The learner distinguishes the intended audience from at least one adjacent audience and articulates what each would prefer differently.
The learner adapts vocabulary, examples, format, or length in ways visible in the artifact (not only described in reflection) to fit the named audience.

The learner designs for a defined primary audience while accounting for foreseeable secondary audiences (e.g., archival readers, parents, future learners), and notes choices that serve or fail to serve secondaries.

dimensions.name: Purpose and intent
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner names the change they want the artifact to produce in the audience — to inform, persuade, move, entertain, instruct, provoke — and structures the artifact around that intent.

components.descriptor: The learner names in one phrase what the artifact is for ("to teach," "to make them laugh," "to help them remember").
The learner names purpose and points to at least one form choice (opening, sequence, ending) shaped by that purpose.
The learner defends two or more form choices by reference to purpose and can describe how a different purpose would have produced different choices.

The learner holds purpose stable while exploring multiple possible forms, selects among them with explicit tradeoff analysis, and can articulate why the chosen form serves the purpose better than alternatives considered.

dimensions.name: Expression and medium
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner uses the medium's specific affordances — what it can do that other mediums cannot — rather than treating the medium as a neutral container.

components.descriptor: The learner tries a medium and notices, with prompting, something the medium can do (e.g., "music can make it sad").
The learner uses at least one medium-specific affordance (color, sound, motion, layout, pacing) intentionally and can name why.
The learner uses medium-specific affordances in service of stated purpose and audience, not for novelty alone.
The learner combines affordances across mediums or sub-mediums (e.g., type and image, sound and silence, code and prose) and defends the combination as serving purpose better than either alone.

dimensions.name: Critique and response
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner solicits, receives, and acts on critique without collapsing into compliance or defensiveness, and gives critique to peers in terms that serve the work.

components.descriptor: The learner receives feedback without distress and tries at least one suggestion.
The learner asks for feedback on a specific aspect of the work (a specific question, not "what do you think") and acts on at least one piece received.
The learner distinguishes compliance, defense, and negotiation in their own responses to critique and can name a recent instance of each.
The learner gives critique to peers that names what is working and what is not, in terms the maker can act on, distinct from praise or correction.

domains.name: Building
domains.description: Practice of constructing a structure or system from components such that it functions reliably under specified conditions.

dimensions.name: Materials and medium reasoning
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner selects materials or components based on the demands of the build, names tradeoffs (cost, weight, durability, availability, complexity), and revises material choices in response to test results.

components.descriptor: The learner picks from offered materials and explains, when asked, why the choice was made.
The learner compares at least two materials on one trait (strength, color, cost, weight, availability) before selecting.
The learner selects materials by at least two tradeoffs and revises material choice in response to test results.
The learner documents material choices with quantitative or comparative evidence and considers lifecycle factors (sourcing, durability, end-of-life) appropriate to the project.

dimensions.name: Structure and systems thinking
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner organizes components into a structure with named relationships, identifies points of stress or coupling, and uses that structure to predict behavior before testing.

components.descriptor: The learner names at least two parts of the build and how they connect.
The learner produces a diagram of the build with parts and connections labeled.
The learner identifies at least one stress point, fragile coupling, or single point of failure in the structure and addresses it in the design.
The learner predicts system behavior from structure before test and explains any observed deviation in terms of the structure post-test.
Before making the parts, the learner says how two of them will join — what will touch what — and then makes the parts so they fit.

components.descriptor: Before building, the learner writes or draws what has to be true where two parts meet (size, shape, order, what is passed across), then checks the finished parts against that description.

components.descriptor: The learner specifies in advance what each side of a boundary between two parts must provide and what each may assume, so that either part can be changed without rebuilding the other, and reports whether a part built to the specification fitted.

dimensions.name: Durability and robustness
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner anticipates conditions of use — including misuse, edge cases, and time — and designs for them, then tests against those conditions.

components.descriptor: The learner uses the build more than once and notices when something breaks or fails.
The learner tests the build under at least one non-trivial condition (rougher use, longer time, harsher environment).
The learner tests against at least one misuse case the learner imagined (not only the intended use) and reports the result.
The learner designs and reports failure tests, specifies the operating envelope within which the build is intended to function, and notes the boundary conditions.

dimensions.name: Function and fit-for-use
dimensions.anchorStatement: The learner evaluates the build against its stated function in the hands of intended users, accepts the gap between intent and result as data, and decides whether the gap warrants revision.

components.descriptor: The learner gives the build to a user and watches what happens.
The learner records whether the user could use the build as intended and names at least one gap between intent and use.
The learner iterates on observed-not-asked evidence (what the user did, not what the user said) and distinguishes user error from design error.
The learner defines fit-for-use criteria before testing, reports against them after, and recommends specific next-revision changes with reasons.

A three-year ethnography of hobbyist rocketry, not a K-12 study; grounds no band placement.
